executive_summary: GBP/CHF trades at 1.09224 (payload close, 3 September 2026), up 0.47% over one month, 2.63% over three, 4.40% over six and 1.83% over twelve — a persistent, decelerating uptrend that has carried the cross from 1.04027 on 6 March to the 87th percentile of its 52-week closing range. The dominant bilateral narrative is the widest liquid carry gap in the G10 that its low-yield leg has no capacity to close: Bank Rate at 3.75% against an SNB policy rate of 0.00%, a 375bp differential the Swiss National Bank has effectively pre-committed to preserving by conditioning its entire three-year inflation forecast on a zero policy rate. The observed futures roll of -406.8bp annualised means a rolled long earns roughly 4.07% a year — 375bp of policy plus about 32bp of basis — against a pair implied volatility estimate of 4.753%, and Bank of America has argued the uptrend has further to run on the grounds that no major G10 cross offers higher vol-adjusted carry. What diverges most sharply from the standalone dossiers is the direction of the rate factor: sterling is Bearish on its own book because the Fed and ECB are moving above it, and neither is the counterparty here, while the franc is Bearish on its own book for a reason — a zero rate — that is precisely what makes this cross work. Against that sit three fundamental negatives that the carry cannot argue with: a 12.6 percentage point current-account differential (Switzerland +9.77% of GDP against the UK -2.84%), a AAA sovereign at 37.6% debt-to-GDP facing a AA one at 95.1% with a dated Budget on 28 October, and Swiss data beating consensus by a full percentage point on Q2 GDP while UK retail sales collapse. The settled verdict is tactically Bullish at conviction 2 and strategically Neutral at conviction 2; our caveat, which the chart supports and the score deliberately did not see, is that the 200-week average sits 123 pips overhead at 1.10452 and the 2 September high of 1.10084 was the first lower high of the entire six-month sequence — so the tactical upside is structurally capped tighter than a +0.1814 score implies, and the honest content of both horizons is the carry rather than the spot move.

market_context.valuation_assessment: There is no purchasing-power-parity source for this cross, and none is asserted. The available proxy is the relative BIS real effective exchange rate: sterling's broad REER is 111.41 for June 2026 against Switzerland's 101.69, a 9.56% gap that would imply a GBP/CHF near 1.0000 if the two real rates were equalised. That is a REER-relative proxy and not a fair-value model output — both dossiers label it as such, both underlying REER readings are for June 2026 and roughly 63 days old at the valuation date, and the Swiss percentile is computed on a 30-month window only. What the proxy does say, and it is worth saying plainly, is that the pair is expensive on the only trade-weighted measure available at the same time as its 52-week closing percentile is 87 — a currency pair does not have to mean-revert to a REER-parity level, but a 9% premium caps how much further a carry trade can extend before valuation becomes a constraint rather than a footnote. Against that, sterling's REER has declined 2.73 points over a year and the franc's 1.03 points, so the real-rate gap has been widening rather than closing, which is exactly what has driven the six-month move. One market-data provider notes GBP/CHF trading in a very stable 4.0% range over the recent quarter, which is consistent with the payload's 4.78% 60-day realised volatility and reinforces that this has been a grind rather than a repricing.

positioning.net_pair_implication: On a relative reading sterling is the more heavily short leg, which is a mild bullish tilt for the pair, but both short bases have been covering simultaneously and the fuel is being consumed rather than accumulated. The internal composition cuts in opposite directions: sterling's fast money is already long (leveraged funds 40,670 contracts, 15.9% of open interest) while the franc's leveraged funds are short 11,432, so the fast-money community is long this pair and amplifying rather than muting; real money is short both legs. The structural flow reading is a liquidation-prone leveraged long in the base against a concentrated, slow-moving real-money short in the quote — a configuration that absorbs nothing and amplifies everything around a dated sterling event.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime since March has been a pure carry grind: sterling's wide interest-rate advantage over the franc has driven the move, with the pair gaining roughly 1.4% from the start of July as the higher yield encouraged investors to fund positions through the low-yielding Swiss currency, while uncertainty over further Bank of England tightening has limited the case for an unchecked advance. The regime's defining characteristic is orderliness rather than force — 60-day realised volatility of 4.78% and a 55-pip ATR on a pair that has travelled 4.40% in six months. The contradiction underneath is that Switzerland's own fundamentals have been the strongest in years and none of them buys a rate rise at 0.4% headline inflation, while Britain's have been deteriorating and the market cannot mark down sterling's carry because the BoE cannot cut into 2.9% CPI. The regime broke character twice in three weeks — the 19 August CPI session and the 2 September failed high — and both breaks were sterling-negative, the first evidence in six months that the carry is no longer doing all the work.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The bilateral policy differential is +375bp: Bank Rate at 3.75% as of 28 August against an SNB policy rate of 0.00% as of 1 September — the third-widest gap the franc faces in its own benchmarking set and the widest sterling owns against any liquid G10 counterparty. The observed futures calendar-spread roll premium is -406.8bp annualised on the CHF-base orientation, so a rolled long GBP/CHF earns roughly +4.07% annualised, decomposing by covered interest parity into the 375bp interest differential plus roughly 32bp of cross-currency basis that currently works in favour of a long — it is cheap to fund the franc and hold sterling. The carry regime is working, and working through the classic funding-currency channel rather than through risk appetite alone: VIX is 14.51, US investment grade 79bp and high yield 263bp, and the franc is the only zero rate in the G10, with the SNB signalling a hold at 0% through 2026 and a high bar to returning to negative rates. The regime breaks on realised volatility rather than on policy — 20-day realised at 6.11% against 60-day at 4.78% is the first crack, and the carry-to-vol ratio deteriorates from roughly 0.78 (60-day realised) to roughly 0.61 (20-day realised) as that volatility rises. The cushion (breakeven move) is real and the best available on a liquid cross, but it is nowhere near large enough to absorb a Budget accident.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Bank Rate is 3.75% and the SNB policy rate is 0.00%, a 375bp bilateral differential that is the third-widest the franc faces and the widest sterling owns against any liquid G10 counterparty other than the franc itself. The critical bilateral point is that this differential has no scheduled path to compression inside four weeks. The gated calendar puts the BoE on 17 September with roughly +7bp priced and a Reuters poll of 13-18 August finding 56 of 64 economists expecting no change for the rest of 2026, and the SNB on 24 September at a quarterly assessment whose June conditional inflation forecast of 0.6% for 2026, 0.6% for 2027 and 0.7% for 2028 is explicitly conditioned on the policy rate remaining at 0% across the entire three-year horizon. Sterling's dossier is Bearish on this factor because the Fed and ECB are moving above it; neither of those banks is the counterparty here, and the compression that damages GBP/USD and EUR/GBP does nothing to the 375bp franc gap. Transmission is direct and mechanical: the funding block prints a calendar-spread roll premium of -406.8bp annualised on the CHF-base orientation, meaning a rolled long GBP/CHF earns roughly 4.07% annualised, decomposing into 375bp of policy differential plus about 32bp that is cross-currency basis and cannot be separated without an OIS curve. Against a pair 3m ATM implied volatility of 4.753% that is a carry-to-vol ratio of 0.789, the best risk-adjusted carry in either dossier's cross-section.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the level of the differential still favours the pair heavily but the trajectory turns mildly against it, and the asymmetry is entirely on the sterling leg. The plausible six-month distribution for Bank Rate is 3.50% to 4.00%: three standing hawks in Greene, Mann and Pill voted for 4.00% at the 29 July meeting, while Taylor argues the economy is drifting toward deficient demand and Ramsden's guidance is explicitly two-way, with the decisive input — 2027 pay settlements — arriving at the 5 November Monetary Policy Report and the 17 December decision. Private-sector regular pay at 2.8% and unemployment at 4.9% and rising lean the resolution dovish. The Swiss leg has no distribution worth speaking of: headline CPI is 0.4% and core 0.3%, the SNB's own forecast is conditioned on 0% through 2028, and the 24 September and 10 December assessments are near-certain holds. So the bilateral differential most likely ends the horizon between 350bp and 400bp rather than converging, and the pair still accrues roughly 190bp of carry over six months. That is a real, positive, non-price return, which is why this factor stays Bullish even though the direction of change is mildly adverse; confidence falls from 70 to 55 precisely because the only movement available is compression.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth differential and the surprise differential both run against the pair right now, and the surprise differential runs against it hard. Switzerland delivered Q2 GDP of +1.5% quarter-on-quarter on SECO's flash against an AWP consensus of +0.2% to +0.4%, a KOF barometer of 106.7 against a 103.0 forecast and its highest reading since November 2021, and industrial production of +5.5% year-on-year against a -4.7% forecast — a 10.2 point beat. The United Kingdom, by contrast, is producing a data set that contradicts itself: Q2 GDP +0.4% quarter-on-quarter and +1.2% year-on-year with August flash composite PMI at 52.5, set against retail sales -0.5% month-on-month with the annual rate collapsing to 1.6% from 3.8% and a CBI distributive trades print of -48 against -35 expected. On the OECD vintages Swiss GDP runs +2.33% year-on-year against the UK's +1.2%. The inflation differential points the other way and is the reason this is only a moderate Bearish rather than a strong one: UK CPI of 2.9% against Swiss CPI of 0.4% gives sterling a real policy rate of +0.85% against the franc's -0.40%, a 125bp real carry advantage. Transmission at four weeks is through equity and direct-investment flows into the outperforming economy and through the surprise index itself, not through relative policy, because neither central bank's reaction function is live to these prints. The 16 September UK CPI is the swing release, and its energy-driven upside skew is genuinely ambiguous for the pair — it raises the BoE's hawkish tail while taxing UK real income.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Extend the horizon and the growth differential converges rather than widens, which is why the honest strategic stance is Neutral. The Swiss surge is very likely borrowed: US Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs of up to 15% were announced on 2 April 2026 and took effect on 31 July, Roche and Novartis are shielded for three years and no one else is, pharmaceuticals are close to half of Swiss goods exports to the United States, and July chemical and pharmaceutical exports jumped 25.7% — front-running whose payback lands in Q4 2026 and Q1 2027, inside this window. The IMF's June Article IV puts Swiss growth at 0.8% for 2026 and the SNB at around 1%, both far below the run-rate implied by a +1.5% quarter. On the sterling side the deterioration is slower but genuine and points one way: unemployment at 4.9% and up 0.2 points on the year, payrolled employees down 210,000, vacancies at 705,000 and the lowest since early 2021, private-sector regular pay decelerating to 2.8% and real regular pay growth of only +0.5%. So both legs slow, from very different starting points, and the differential closes towards zero from the Swiss side while the level of UK activity erodes from below. Inflation adds nothing directional: Swiss inflation is too low to move policy and UK inflation is high enough to prevent cuts but not to force hikes. Neither half of the mandate generates a bilateral signal at this horizon.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Bearish tactically to Neutral strategically because the same figures mean different things at different lags. tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is a carry cross with a haven on the quote side, so the risk regime maps onto it almost one-for-one, and the current regime is as supportive as it gets. VIX closed at 14.51 on 27 August, down 3.70 points on the month from 18.21 and near its 2026 low; US investment-grade spreads are 79bp and high-yield 263bp, the latter 21bp tighter on the month; US equities are at record highs and the FTSE 100 finished around 10,815 on 28 August, up roughly 20% on the year. In that tape the franc's structural bid is absent and its funding-currency role dominates, while sterling's mild positive risk beta works with rather than against the differential. The bilateral asymmetry is that both legs push the same way: risk-on removes the franc's haven premium at the same time as it rewards holding the higher-yielding leg. The one dissenting cross-asset signal, and it is a real one, is gold at 4,456 and up 8.60% on the month and 22.39% on the year — the franc's traditional correlate is being bought hard while the franc is sold, which is a correlation breakdown rather than confirmation and suggests franc haven demand is being under-bid rather than extinguished. Confidence is 60 rather than higher because a 14.51 VIX leaves essentially no cushion, and because the compression that has driven the pair's carry regime cannot repeat from here.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the risk factor stops being a direction and becomes a distribution, and for this pair the distribution is genuinely two-sided in expectation even though it is strongly skewed in shape. If the current regime simply persists, the pair collects 375bp of carry and grinds — the modal outcome and a positive one. If volatility rises, the pair is hit on both legs simultaneously: the franc receives the haven bid while sterling faces an energy-driven terms-of-trade shock and a fiscal event, which is precisely the configuration in which GBP/CHF falls fastest. With VIX at 14.51 and high-yield at 263bp there is far more room for volatility to widen than to compress, the Middle East conflict that produced a 30-dollar Brent round trip between June and August is unresolved, and the SNB itself names the risk of strong franc appreciation as its principal concern. Two things stop this becoming an outright Bearish call. First, the SNB's stated increased willingness to intervene truncates the right tail of any franc rally, backed by CHF 889.6bn of official reserve assets. Second, sterling's dominant six-month risk is domestic and fiscal rather than global, so VIX simply will not forecast the 28 October Budget — the informational value of this factor for the pair falls as the horizon lengthens. A supportive modal path against a fat, policy-truncated adverse tail nets to Neutral at a 0.05 weight.

Over the strategic window the same compression is the reason the factor cannot be extrapolated — there is far more room to widen than to tighten, and a widening hits both legs of this pair in the same direction.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Speculators are net short both legs, which is the configuration in which the pair signal is muted rather than amplified. Sterling's headline non-commercial net was -44,500 contracts on the 28 August release, improved from -54,600 the prior week and at roughly the 30th percentile of its one-year distribution; the franc's all-speculator net was -19.9k, having covered from -32.5k in three weeks, at roughly the 48th percentile of its own band. On a relative reading sterling is the more heavily short leg, which is a mild bullish tilt for the pair, but both short bases have been covering simultaneously and the covering fuel on both sides is being consumed rather than accumulated. The internal composition matters more than the headlines and cuts in opposite directions: sterling's fast money is already long at 40,670 leveraged-fund contracts, 15.9% of open interest and up from 6.4% on 7 July, while the franc's residual short is concentrated in asset managers at -38,322 against total open interest of only 109,874. So the marginal buyer of sterling has largely finished buying while the marginal buyer of francs is a slow real-money hedger who does not respond to headlines. There is no bilateral extreme in either direction, no pair-specific crowding measure available, and no dated trigger inside four weeks, so Neutral at 50 is the honest reading rather than a failure to choose.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the positioning question changes from whether either leg is stretched to what happens to each position if something goes wrong, and the answer is asymmetric against the pair. Sterling enters the 28 October Budget with leveraged funds net long 40,670 contracts, which means a disappointing Budget forces liquidation of existing longs on top of any fresh shorting — the 2022 analogue, when sterling fell roughly 8% against the dollar in the fortnight around the mini-Budget precisely because the market was not short going in. The franc enters the same window with a concentrated real-money short of 38,322 contracts against total open interest of only 109,874, which is squeeze fuel rather than an overhang, with dealers as the long counterparty at +62,382. The structural flow channels reinforce the same asymmetry: the LDI/pension hedge-ratio channel that transmitted the 2022 gilt crisis is live with the 30-year gilt at 5.73-5.76% and overseas investors holding 25-30% of outstanding gilts, while a 9.77%-of-GDP Swiss current account and a CHF 974bn net international investment position produce a continuous, price-insensitive franc bid. A liquidation-prone long in the base against a squeeze-prone short in the quote is a Bearish configuration for the pair, and the honest limit on confidence is that the trigger is exogenous and undated.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Strategic weight raised from the 0.16 default. The two economies are near mirror images on the external account — Switzerland at +9.77% of GDP against the United Kingdom at -2.84%, a 12.6 percentage point differential — and the same energy shock that produces a record Swiss trade surplus is a direct income transfer out of Britain. That is the largest bilateral fundamental gap in this pair and the framework's justification for a commodity-and-external overweight applies squarely.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The external differential is the widest single fundamental gap in this pair and it deteriorated further during August. The United Kingdom ran a current account deficit of GBP 22.1bn in Q1 2026, 2.8% of GDP, with the goods deficit widening GBP 4.0bn to GBP 59.5bn while the offsetting services surplus fell GBP 1.2bn to GBP 51.8bn; the headline narrowing came entirely from a volatile GBP 8.0bn primary income swing. Switzerland ran CHF 16bn in the same quarter, 9.77% of GDP, and then posted a July trade surplus of CHF 8.1bn, the largest since the series began in January 1950, on exports up 13.8% and imports down 4.5%. On the commodity channel both currencies are net energy importers, but the intensities and the direction of the shock are not symmetric: UK front-month NBP gas settled at 161.02 pence per therm on 26 August and around 165 on 28 August, 18-21% above the Bank of England's own 136-pence July conditioning assumption and about 43% higher on the year, while Brent's fall from 100.31 to 88.24 is a terms-of-trade gain that accrues to the less energy-intensive Swiss economy at least as much as to Britain. Gold, the franc's principal commodity correlate, is up 8.60% on the month and 22.39% on the year. Bilaterally, IMF DOTS puts UK exports to Switzerland at USD 9.3bn against imports of USD 12.8bn in 2024, a net UK goods deficit of USD 3.5bn — a small but structurally franc-positive flow. Transmission at four weeks is slow, which is why the weight stays at 0.06, but the direction is not in doubt.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.19 weight this is the second-largest strategic contributor and the highest-confidence bearish leg in the pair, because the mechanism is arithmetic rather than expectational. Switzerland's 9.77%-of-GDP current account is the product of a goods surplus in pharmaceuticals, precision engineering and watches, a services and commodity-trading surplus, and a primary income surplus thrown off by a net international investment position of CHF 974bn, roughly 120% of annual GDP. Britain's -2.84% is the product of a 7.6%-of-GDP goods deficit that energy prices drive and a shrinking financial services surplus that is supposed to offset it, with post-Brexit barriers having structurally reduced trade openness. Over one to six months the United Kingdom must sell sterling continuously to buy energy while Switzerland must absorb or recycle a continuous franc inflow, and the northern hemisphere heating season falls inside the window with European storage refill competing against Asian LNG buyers and the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed. Two genuine offsets keep confidence at 72 rather than higher. First, the 15% Section 232 pharmaceutical tariff plus Switzerland's commitment to facilitate at least USD 200bn of investment into the United States over five years, USD 67bn of it in 2026, is a real outbound offset that will shrink the Swiss surplus at the margin — the Q1 current account was already CHF 11bn below a year earlier. Second, a durable Hormuz reopening would collapse the UK energy bill and is the single most pair-bullish event available, assessed at roughly 20%.

factors.horizon_split: Both horizons are Bearish, with strategic confidence of 72 against tactical 60 and the weight tripling from 0.06 to 0.19, because balance-of-payments flows are cumulative. Over four weeks a record Swiss surplus and an 18-21% gas overshoot are headlines. Over one to six months they are a measured income transfer that shows up in the Q3 and Q4 balance of payments, in the UK energy price cap and in the heating season that falls inside the window — exactly the horizon at which a 12.6 percentage point current account differential binds.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: Sterling: net energy importer with a 2.8%-of-GDP current account deficit and a 7.6%-of-GDP goods deficit. Direction rules give oil up as negative for GBP and NBP gas up as strongly negative for GBP, and the UK is uniquely exposed on the gas leg because NBP is the pricing point for both the household energy price cap and industrial costs. UK NBP gas is 161-165 pence per therm against the BoE's own 136-pence conditioning assumption.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: Franc: also a net energy importer, but far less energy-intensive per unit of GDP and running a 9.77%-of-GDP current account surplus that absorbs the shock. The franc's dominant commodity correlate is gold, where direction rules give gold up as positive for CHF and where Switzerland is the world's largest refining hub; gold is +8.60% on the month and +22.39% on the year. Swiss export composition is pharmaceuticals, precision engineering and watches, none of which is commodity-priced.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Take the framework rules leg by leg. Gas up: strongly negative for GBP through both the price cap and industrial costs, mildly negative for CHF given lower energy intensity and a surplus that absorbs it — net clearly BEARISH for GBP/CHF, and this is the live channel with gas 18-21% above the BoE's baseline. Oil down 12.0% on the month: mildly positive for GBP as an importer, mildly positive for CHF as an importer, with the Swiss gain larger per unit of GDP because the Swiss economy carries no offsetting energy production — net marginally BEARISH for the pair. Gold up: neutral for GBP, positive for CHF through both the haven correlation and the refining channel — net BEARISH. All three channels point the same way, which is unusual and is why this factor is the highest-confidence bearish leg in the pair.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Brent from 88.24 to roughly 97 dollars, most plausibly on Hormuz re-escalation, would almost certainly drag NBP gas higher with it. GBP takes a double hit through the import bill and the real-income channel while the risk-off component simultaneously bids the franc; CHF takes a smaller terms-of-trade hit offset by haven demand. Net: materially BEARISH GBP/CHF, and the single cleanest adverse scenario for the pair because it moves both legs the same way.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Brent from 88.24 to roughly 79 dollars, most plausibly on a durable Hormuz reopening, would collapse the UK energy import bill while leaving Bank Rate at 3.75% — the base dossier's single most sterling-positive combination, assessed at roughly 20% probability. CHF would lose part of its haven and gold bid at the same time. Net: BULLISH GBP/CHF, and the principal invalidator of this factor.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: UK front-month NBP natural gas. It is the only commodity in the set that is asymmetric between the two legs at the current level — 18-21% above the Bank of England's own conditioning assumption, in a fuel Britain must import and Switzerland barely uses — and it is the channel through which the 2026 energy shock becomes a sterling-specific rather than a shared cost.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Strategic weight trimmed from the 0.12 default. The two banks' guidance points in opposite directions for this pair — the SNB explicitly caps its own currency, which is pair-supportive, while the BoE's symmetric reaction function most likely resolves dovish at the 5 November Monetary Policy Report, which is pair-negative — so part of the factor's normal strategic weight is self-cancelling and belongs with External Balance and Fiscal, where the bilateral gap is unambiguous.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The guidance asymmetry on this pair is unusually clean. The SNB's 18 June assessment states that, if necessary, it has an increased willingness to intervene in the foreign exchange market to counter a rapid and excessive appreciation of the franc, and Chairman Schlegel reaffirmed that formulation on 8 July while noting medium-term inflationary pressure was virtually unchanged. That is one-sided language: there is no corresponding commitment against franc weakness, and no plausible level of depreciation at which a bank forecasting 0.6% inflation would object. For a GBP/CHF holder that is a written option on the quote leg — the central bank has said it will sell the currency you are short if it rallies hard and will do nothing if it falls. The Bank of England offers nothing comparable in either direction: the 29 July minutes are the most explicitly two-sided communication of the cycle, with Ramsden stating a hike may be warranted if risks crystallise and that he would consider resuming cuts if they subside, Taylor openly dovish, and Mann and Pill arguing Bank Rate should be above 3.75%. Sequencing favours the pair mildly: the BoE decides on 17 September, a week before the SNB on 24 September, so a priced BoE hold sets the tone and the SNB assessment is the live communication event. Confidence is held at 55 rather than higher precisely because that assessment is genuinely two-sided — after a six-month franc depreciation the pressure the intervention sentence was written to counter has abated, and dropping or softening it would be read as tolerance of a stronger franc.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two guidance regimes partially offset, and the residual favours the pair only narrowly. On the franc side the SNB's structural incentive to prefer a softer currency is reinforced rather than weakened by the 15% Section 232 pharmaceutical tariff, since a levy on close to half of Swiss goods exports to the United States raises the cost of any further competitiveness loss through the exchange rate; the stated tool preference is intervention rather than negative rates, with Schlegel repeatedly citing the undesirable side effects of sub-zero policy; and the assessments on 24 September and 10 December are the only scheduled communication points. On the sterling side the reaction function is symmetric and credible but its decisive input — 2027 pay settlements — arrives at the 5 November Monetary Policy Report and the 17 December decision, and the incoming evidence leans dovish with private-sector regular pay at 2.8%, DMP year-ahead wage expectations at 3.4% and three-year CPI expectations at 2.8%. A dovish resolution is worth at most 25bp against a 375bp gap, so it is a smaller factor than the SNB's explicit cap, but it is a real offset and is why confidence falls from 55 to 52. The credibility differential is genuine but two-sided: the SNB is the more operationally credible institution on FX, with the January 2015 floor removal the standing reminder that its guidance does not bind indefinitely, while the BoE's post-2022 transparency framework is intact.

Tactically the asymmetry is at its sharpest: a priced BoE hold on 17 September followed by an SNB assessment whose one-sided intervention language is the only live text in the window. tactical.bilateral_analysis: Inside four weeks neither leg carries a genuine binary and the dated events are clustered but scheduled. On the sterling side the calendar is 11 September monthly GDP and trade, 15 September the labour market report, 16 September August CPI, 17 September the MPC decision with its annual gilt-reduction vote and 18 September retail sales — dense, but every item is a scheduled release with a published consensus, and the Budget date is fixed at 28 October, outside the window. On the franc side the dated item is the 27 September federal referendum on constitutionally entrenching neutrality; Tamedia polling from late August has 62% against and 36% in favour, so rejection is the strong base case and the modal outcome is a non-event, with roughly a 20% passage tail whose franc direction is itself ambiguous. The 24 September SNB assessment is a communication event rather than a policy binary. The one undated risk that matters more for this pair than for either currency alone is the Middle East: a re-escalation bids the franc as a haven at the same moment it taxes Britain's energy import bill, so the two legs move together rather than offsetting. Over four weeks its probability-weighted contribution is small, and the honest tactical stance is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Extend the window and the event risk becomes both dated and one-sided. The Autumn Budget on 28 October, with an accompanying OBR economic and fiscal forecast, is delivered by a Chancellor appointed three weeks before the date was set, under a Prime Minister who took office on 20 July, against an OBR March headroom figure of GBP 9.9bn that the OBR itself warned could be erased by a modest rise in borrowing costs — and the 10-year gilt has since risen 39bp on the year at roughly GBP 2.5bn of annual debt service per 0.25 percentage point. The distribution around it is skewed against the pair because the fiscal rules cap the good outcome while a 5.73-5.76% 30-year yield amplifies the bad one. Switzerland's equivalent event set is materially benign: the neutrality referendum most likely fails, Bilaterals III was signed on 2 March 2026 with a clear majority of consultation respondents supportive, and the genuinely Swiss-negative item — the Section 232 pharmaceutical tariff regime — is already in force and already visible in the trade data. The asymmetry that matters most is that the two largest tails point the same way: a Hormuz re-escalation and a disorderly Budget both push GBP/CHF lower, and there is no symmetric scenario in which a Swiss event pushes it higher by a comparable magnitude.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Raised from the 0.04 and 0.07 defaults. This is the framework's designated background factor, but not on this pair: it joins the developed world's widest sovereign risk premium — a gilt-Bund spread of 184bp, the widest since the 2022 mini-Budget, with net debt at 95.1% of GDP — directly to a AAA sovereign at 37.6% debt-to-GDP with a constitutional debt brake, and a dated fiscal binary falls inside the strategic window.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The sovereign differential on this pair is close to the largest available in the G10 and it is currently live rather than background. The United Kingdom carries public sector net debt of 95.1% of GDP at end-May 2026, the highest since the early 1960s, ratings of AA at S&P and AA- at Fitch with the Moody's level reported variously as Aa2 or Aa3 and no confirmable outlook, a 10-year gilt at 5.16% and a 30-year at 5.73-5.76% within 5bp of its May multi-decade peak, and a gilt-Bund spread of about 184bp that is the widest since the 2022 mini-Budget. Switzerland is rated AAA by every major agency, reconfirmed by Morningstar DBRS with a stable trend on 16 January 2026, carries general government debt of 37.6% of GDP on the rating-agency measure, runs an estimated fiscal surplus of 0.4% of GDP under a constitutional debt brake, and funds itself at 0.31% at the 10-year with negligible Confederation supply. The transmission that matters here is the regime-dependent correlation the base dossier flags: cable and other sterling crosses are normally positively correlated with the 30-year gilt yield, but the sign flips in a fiscal event, and a long yield entrenched at a multi-decade extreme is the flipped configuration. The gilt market has priced UK fiscal risk aggressively and the currency has not.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: This is the highest-confidence bearish leg in the pair after External Balance, and the reason is that the arithmetic is closed and adverse on one leg while being closed and favourable on the other. tactical.bilateral_analysis: Global dollar funding is abundant and orderly, and for a carry cross with a zero-rate quote leg that is a tailwind rather than a comfort. SOFR printed 3.65% inside the 3.50-3.75% target range with no dislocation, quantitative tightening ended after roughly USD 2.2trn of runoff with reserve balances near USD 2.99trn, and the three-month EUR/USD basis — the benchmark for dollar scarcity — was last observed at only -16 to -20bp against a -35 to -45bp regime through 2023, although that reading is mid-May 2026 and roughly 110 days old, breaching both freshness windows. The bilateral consequence is that CHF-funded carry positions stay financed, and GBP/CHF at a 375bp differential is one of the most direct expressions of that trade in the G10. The pair-specific basis is better evidence than the generic dollar plumbing: the gated funding block prints -406.8bp annualised on the CHF-base orientation against a 375bp policy differential, implying roughly 32bp of basis that currently works in favour of a long GBP/CHF rather than against it. The base dossier's Bearish read on this factor is a statement about the dollar leg of cable after Chair Warsh's 28 August Jackson Hole address moved September hike odds from 36% to 58-60%; on this cross that repricing is close to neutral, because a hawkish Fed raises the global cost of the funding currency and the franc is the funding currency. Confidence is only 52 because the broad dollar has fallen 2.1% on the month even as the Fed turned hawkish, which muddies the channel.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two halves of this factor pull against each other on this specific cross and the honest answer is Neutral. On the supportive side, dollar liquidity is likely to stay easy — the Fed balance sheet is flat to marginally growing, reserve-management purchases rather than renewed runoff are expected, and the basis shows no scarcity premium — which keeps franc-funded carry positions financed and is pair-supportive. On the adverse side, 31 December is the largest recurring dollar-funding squeeze in the calendar and it falls inside the window; a classic year-end basis widening forces a reduction of exactly the CHF-funded positions this pair depends on, and with the EUR/USD basis last seen at only -16 to -20bp there is more room than usual for it to widen. The base leg carries an additional strategic exposure that has no franc equivalent: London's role in global banking makes UK institutions structurally large dollar borrowers, so a year-end funding turn stresses the sterling side of this cross more than the Swiss side. Netting an easy funding backdrop against a seasonal squeeze that hits the pair on both legs leaves no direction, and at a reduced 0.07 weight this factor correctly contributes nothing to the strategic score.

Policy & Rates contributes +0.1890 on its own — more than the entire net score — with Risk Appetite (+0.0720), Guidance (+0.0385) and USD Liquidity (+0.0364) adding a further +0.1469 of the same underlying trade: hold the 375bp differential while volatility is compressed, dollars are abundant and the quote leg's central bank says it will lean against its own currency's strength. tactical.rationale: At tactical weights Policy & Rates carries 0.27 and Inflation & Growth 0.15, so 42% of the score sits with two factors that point in opposite directions, and the rate factor wins because it is the one with no scheduled mechanism to move. The bilateral differential is 375bp, the gated calendar puts the BoE on 17 September with roughly +7bp priced and the SNB on 24 September with a hold effectively certain, and the SNB's June conditional inflation forecast is explicitly conditioned on a 0% policy rate through 2028 — so the gap that matters here is structurally unable to close from the quote side. That is the central bilateral insight and it is what separates this cross from the base dossier's own view: sterling is Bearish standalone because the Fed and ECB are moving above it, and neither of those banks is the counterparty. The observed futures roll of -406.8bp annualised on the CHF-base orientation means a rolled long earns roughly 4.07% a year, 375bp of policy plus about 32bp of basis, against a pair 3m implied volatility estimate of 4.753% — a carry-to-vol ratio of 0.789, the best in either dossier. Three factors reinforce that same trade: a 14.51 VIX with high yield at 263bp, abundant dollar funding with SOFR at 3.65% and no quarter-end in the window, and an SNB that has told the market twice since June it will counter a rapid franc appreciation while the BoE says nothing about sterling at all. The conflict is genuine and it is Switzerland's own fundamentals: Q2 GDP of +1.5% quarter-on-quarter against a +0.2% to +0.4% consensus, a KOF barometer at a four-and-a-half-year high of 106.7, industrial production beating by 10.2 points, a record CHF 8.1bn July trade surplus and a 9.77%-of-GDP current account against Britain's -2.84%. None of it buys a Swiss rate rise at 0.4% headline inflation, which is exactly why it scores -0.0825 rather than more. What is priced is both holds; what is not priced is that a 375bp differential with no scheduled compression pays roughly 31bp a month while the pair's volatility surface charges nothing extra for the September cluster. The path of least resistance over four weeks is therefore a carry grind rather than a trend, with the 16 September UK CPI and the 24 September SNB statement text as the two-way risks. Conviction is 2 rather than 3 for three specific reasons: the score is 104% attributable to one factor; the fundamental negatives are the ones that compound over time rather than decay; and the franc's short base has already covered 40% in three weeks while sterling's leveraged funds are already long 15.9% of open interest, so the flow cushion on both legs has been spent. Second-pass note, offered as disagreement rather than revision: the price payload the first pass did not see tightens this call rather than confirming it. The 2 September high of 1.10084 was the first lower high of the six-month sequence, the declining 200-week average at 1.10452 has capped 237 consecutive weeks, both ten-touch bands on the chart are overhead and there is no ten-touch support anywhere. Nothing in that changes the 375bp differential or the factor scores, and it should not — but it means the Bullish stance should be read as collect the carry inside a range whose ceiling is 1.1088 rather than buy a breakout, which is how the price objectives below are set.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: Among sterling crosses GBP/CHF ranks first or second as a tactical long, because the franc is the only G10 counterparty whose central bank has pre-committed to zero for three years and therefore cannot erode sterling's advantage — the compression that damages GBP/USD and EUR/GBP inside the 10-17 September window simply does not reach this cross. Among franc shorts it ranks third behind AUD/CHF and NOK/CHF on raw carry at 435bp and 425bp, but first on carry-to-vol at 0.789 given GBP/CHF's low realised volatility, and ahead of EUR/CHF on carry while behind it on catalyst density since the ECB is the one bank actually moving. Against GBP/NOK, which the base dossier names the cleanest fundamental sterling short, GBP/CHF is the opposite trade and the ranking gap between them is the widest in the sterling complex. The sell side agrees on the ranking metric if not the horizon: Bank of America argues the pair remains one of the most attractive carry trades in the G10, with quantitative signals turning increasingly positive for sterling.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.0718 sits inside the neutral band of -0.10 to +0.10, and the composition matters far more than the number. This is not ten indifferent factors: it is two large opposing blocs that nearly cancel. The carry-and-guidance bloc contributes +0.2005 — Policy & Rates at +0.1485 on a 375bp differential the quote leg cannot close, plus Guidance at +0.0520 on a central bank that has publicly committed to leaning against its own currency's strength. The structural bloc contributes -0.2723 — External Balance at -0.1368 on a 12.6 percentage point current account differential and an energy shock that taxes only the base leg, Fiscal at -0.0700 on a AA sovereign at 95.1% debt-to-GDP facing a dated Budget against a AAA sovereign at 37.6%, Event Risk at -0.0325 and Flows at -0.0330. Four factors score zero and each is a genuine two-sided assessment. The number is Neutral and it is applied mechanically, but it is Neutral with a bearish tilt of composition: the negative bloc is broader, its two largest components carry the highest confidences in the analysis at 72 and 70, and it is the side that compounds rather than decays. The tie is broken by whether the pair keeps collecting roughly 190bp of carry over six months — which is a question about realised volatility and about 28 October, not about the differential.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the framework moves ten points of weight out of Inflation & Growth, Risk Appetite and USD Liquidity and into External Balance, Guidance and Fiscal, and on this pair those reallocations split rather than align. External Balance rises to 0.19 and is the second-largest contributor at -0.1368 with 72% confidence: Switzerland runs a current account of 9.77% of GDP with a CHF 974bn net international investment position worth roughly 120% of output and posted its largest trade surplus since 1950 in July, while Britain runs -2.84% with a goods deficit widening GBP 4.0bn to 7.6% of GDP and a services surplus that fell GBP 1.2bn in the same quarter — and UK front-month gas at 161-165 pence per therm against the Bank's own 136-pence conditioning assumption is a continuing income transfer out of the base leg with the heating season inside the window. Fiscal at 0.10 adds -0.0700 with 70% confidence, because the gilt market is already charging 184bp over Bunds — the widest since the 2022 mini-Budget — on a sovereign whose OBR headroom of GBP 9.9bn has plausibly been consumed by a 39bp year-on-year rise in yields, against a AAA counterparty funding at 0.31% under a constitutional debt brake. Against that, Policy & Rates holds 0.27 and stays Bullish: the plausible six-month range for the differential is 350-400bp, all of the compression risk sits on the sterling leg, and the pair still accrues roughly 190bp of carry, while Guidance adds +0.0520 because the SNB's asymmetric commitment is reinforced rather than weakened by a 15% Section 232 tariff on close to half of Swiss goods exports to the United States. The factors interact rather than merely summing: the same energy shock that widens Britain's deficit prevents the BoE from cutting, which preserves the carry that props the pair up, while worsening the fiscal arithmetic that the Budget must resolve. What is priced is a modest sterling discount — the cross-implied consensus, derived from GBP/USD medians of 1.33-1.36 and USD/CHF targets of 0.78-0.79, sits roughly 2-4% below spot — and what is not priced anywhere either dossier can find is the terms-of-trade channel as a separate additive negative, or the coincidence that the two fattest tails for this cross point the same way. The path of least resistance is a wide range in which the pair collects carry through September and October and then faces its resolution in the fortnight around 28 October and the 5 November Monetary Policy Report. Conviction is 2 rather than 3 because the score genuinely balances: the carry is real money and the structural deterioration is real too, and calling that a direction would be dishonest arithmetic.

Phase one runs from now to roughly mid-October and should be the pair's better window: the differential is static at 375bp, the carry accrues at roughly 34 pips a month, the September policy cluster resolves with two holds and the pair most plausibly probes but fails at the 1.09830-1.10875 band and the 200-week average at 1.10452. Phase two is the fortnight around 28 October and the 5 November Monetary Policy Report, and it is where the structural bloc gets its hearing — the Budget and its OBR forecast either validate or refute a 184bp gilt-Bund premium, and the base dossier's own path expectation for sterling is a 200-300 pip risk-premium repricing in that window. Between the two, the pair should grind with failed rallies into 1.0980-1.1010 as the market re-tests the top of the range. From November into February the picture bifurcates on a single variable: if the Budget is clean the pair reclaims 1.10452 and the 237-week cap breaks, which is a multi-year regime signal; if it is not, the pair loses 1.08490, has nothing until 1.07348, and the six-touch band at 1.05699-1.06724 becomes the objective. The pattern is best described as a coiled range resolving on a dated fiscal event rather than a V or an L, and the most important structural fact is that the declining 200-week average removes the ambiguity on its own — at the current -0.000215 weekly slope, and with spot in the base case's 1.0900-1.1010 area, the average and the price converge somewhere between 15 and 57 weeks, placing the test inside or just beyond this horizon regardless of what the fundamentals do. Volatility should rise through the window because a bias-adjusted 185.7-day implied near 5.6% is too low for a cross with two jump-prone legs whose jumps coincide.

consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: above the bearish forecast-aggregator consensus on both horizons; below the BofA carry-continuation view on the strategic horizon
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: +130 to +290 pips above the bearish aggregator's 1.0475-1.0722 range; approximately in line to below BofA's unspecified continuation view
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Two reasons, and they are different at each horizon. Tactically, the aggregator consensus reaches its bearish view by combining two single-leg calls without pricing the bilateral differential that connects them — bearish sterling on fiscal risk, which we largely share, and bullish the franc against the dollar on expected Fed easing, which is a dollar view with no bearing on this cross. What that combination drops is the 375bp gap and, critically, the fact that the counterparty central bank has conditioned its own three-year forecast on zero and stated twice since June that it will lean against franc strength. A short GBP/CHF pays away roughly 190bp over six months to hold a fundamentally correct view, and we can find no bearish forecast that charges itself for that. Strategically we differ from BofA in the opposite direction: we weigh the terms-of-trade channel at a 0.19 strategic weight where the carry framing gives it none, and no bank forecast in either dossier prices UK gas at 18-21% above the Bank's own conditioning assumption as a balance-of-payments negative rather than a rate positive.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: Tactically, avoiding a consensus short that would have paid away 34 pips a month while spot ground higher, and collecting roughly 101 pips of expected value over one month. Strategically, avoiding both errors: not shorting a positive-expectancy carry position on a fundamentally correct view, and not leveraging a long into a dated fiscal binary that the 94.7-day volatility tenor prices 0.19 points above a no-event bucket.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the bearish consensus is right and the pair reaches 1.0722 by year-end, our strategic Neutral is wrong by roughly 180 pips of spot, cushioned to about 40 pips net by six months of carry. If BofA is right and the carry continuation runs into the ten-touch bands above 1.11, our strategic Neutral costs the upside — roughly 300 pips — and our tactical target of 1.1010 is 140 pips too conservative. The specific way we are wrong on the bearish side is a UK Budget misstep, which market commentary has previously identified as the trigger capable of taking sterling to a fresh all-time low against the franc.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons are not aligned and the divergence is mechanistic rather than a hedge: four factors change stance between them and each change has an identifiable cause. The tactical Bullish is a bet on a differential that is scheduled to be unchanged and on a regime — compressed volatility, abundant dollars, an intact carry trade — that is time-limited by construction. The strategic Neutral is the recognition that a static 375bp differential stops generating new support and becomes a level, at which point the structural bloc asserts itself: a 12.6 percentage point current account differential, a AAA sovereign facing a AA one with a dated fiscal binary, a leveraged-fund long in the base against a real-money short in the quote, and an energy shock that taxes only the base leg through a heating season that falls inside the window. Inflation & Growth flips from Bearish to Neutral as the Swiss surge proves to be tariff front-running; Risk Appetite flips from Bullish to Neutral as a compressed regime becomes an unreliable six-month signal; Flows flips from Neutral to Bearish as the question changes from whether either leg is stretched to what happens if one has to liquidate; Event Risk flips from Neutral to Bearish as the Budget enters the window.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The fortnight around 28 October 2026, when the Autumn Budget and its OBR forecast either validate or refute a 184bp gilt-Bund premium, followed by the 5 November Bank of England decision with its Monetary Policy Report — the first full forecast round afterwards and the point at which 2027 pay-settlement evidence begins to arrive. In price terms the inflection has a level as well as a date: the 200-week average at 1.10452 and the 1.08490 zone floor are the two boundaries, and the Budget window is the most likely occasion for one of them to break.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The tactical carry view and the strategic structural view are complementary rather than contradictory, but they are not the same position held for different lengths of time. The tactical view has a natural expiry at the 5 November Monetary Policy Report rather than an indefinite roll, and it should be sized to survive a 55-pip ATR and stopped below the 1.08490 zone floor. The strategic view is a statement about a coincident tail on both legs — a haven bid on the franc arriving with an energy and fiscal shock on sterling — which the pair's shallow volatility contango from 4.564% to 4.920% charges nothing for, and it belongs in longer-dated convexity rather than in spot. Because the surface is in contango and not backwardation there is no event premium to decay and therefore no argument for waiting until after the September cluster resolves.

catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council decision with new staff macroeconomic projections
catalysts.rationale: Not in this pair's gated calendar because the ECB is a third-party bank, sourced from the quote dossier rather than searched. A 25bp hike to a 2.50% deposit rate, roughly 97% priced, takes the EUR-CHF policy spread from 225bp to 250bp and drives the franc weaker broadly through the euro cross, lifting GBP/CHF via the quote leg while the sterling differential is static. Explicit confirmation that the cycle is finished would collapse the euro terminal premium and be pair-negative.

catalysts.event: UK labour market report: unemployment, claimant count, average weekly earnings
catalysts.rationale: With unemployment at 4.9% and rising, payrolled employees down 210,000 on the year and private-sector regular pay at 2.8%, a further loosening removes the second-round-effects case that keeps three MPC members voting for 4.00%. On this cross that matters more than usual because the quote leg's rate is pinned at zero, so every basis point of sterling's dovish repricing is a basis point off the 375bp differential with no offset available from the franc side.

catalysts.event: UK August CPI, core CPI and services CPI
catalysts.rationale: July printed 2.9% headline, 2.6% core and 3.4% services, and August carries genuine upside risk from gas at 18-21% above the Bank's July conditioning assumption and BRC shop price inflation at a two-year high of 1.5%. The bilateral ambiguity is sharp: an upside surprise revives the BoE's hawkish tail and widens the differential against a franc that cannot respond, which is pair-bullish, while simultaneously deepening the real-income and terms-of-trade tax that is the pair's strongest bearish leg. The largest single down day of the entire six-month price window — 19 August, a 157-pip range and a 1.0848 close — was the July CPI release, so this pair has demonstrated an asymmetric negative reaction function to UK inflation prints.

catalysts.event: Bank of England MPC decision and minutes with the annual gilt-reduction vote; Swiss trade balance for August the same morning
catalysts.rationale: About +7bp is priced with 56 of 64 economists expecting no change all year, so the rate outcome is discounted and the information is in the vote split and the QT decision — a move from 6-3 to 7-2 thins the hawkish tail that supports the differential, while 5-4 would widen it. The Swiss trade release lands the same morning: a second consecutive surplus near the CHF 8.1bn July record would push the balance-of-payments story into a narrative currently dominated by carry, and both legs therefore report on the same day.

catalysts.event: Swiss National Bank quarterly monetary policy assessment with a refreshed conditional inflation forecast
catalysts.rationale: A hold at 0.00% is effectively certain, so the entire content is in the language: the June statement's increased willingness to intervene against rapid franc appreciation was written when the franc was under upward pressure, and after six months of depreciation that pressure has abated. Dropping or softening the sentence would remove the written cap on the quote leg and is the single most pair-negative outcome available inside the tactical window, worth an estimated 100-150 pips.

catalysts.event: Swiss federal referendum on constitutionally entrenching neutrality
catalysts.rationale: Passage would bar Switzerland from joining sanctions against belligerent states absent a UN Security Council mandate and constrain NATO cooperation, forcing a re-examination of the framework under which CHF 8.5bn of Russian-linked financial assets are frozen. Late-August Tamedia polling at 62% against and 36% in favour makes rejection the strong base case and the modal outcome a non-event; the roughly 20% passage tail is ambiguous for the franc.

catalysts.event: UK Autumn Budget with accompanying OBR economic and fiscal forecast
catalysts.rationale: The single most consequential dated event for this cross over the horizon, and a fiscal rather than a monetary event so it does not appear in the gated calendar. The Chancellor must satisfy fiscal rules whose March headroom of GBP 9.9bn has plausibly been consumed by a 39bp year-on-year rise in the 10-year at roughly GBP 2.5bn of annual debt service per 0.25 percentage point, while the gilt market already charges 184bp over Bunds. The bilateral transmission is the regime-dependent correlation: sterling crosses normally track the 30-year gilt yield positively, but the sign flips in a fiscal event, and the counterparty here is a AAA sovereign funding at 0.31%.

catalysts.event: Bank of England MPC decision with Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.rationale: It is the first full forecast round after the Budget and the meeting at which the three standing hawks vote again with 2027 pay-settlement evidence beginning to arrive; the base dossier assesses a hike here at 25%. Because the Report conditions its forecasts on market-implied rates, its published inflation path is an implicit verdict on whether the market's 2027 timing is right — and on this cross any dovish resolution compresses the 375bp differential with no possible offset from a franc leg pinned at zero.

catalysts.event: Swiss National Bank quarterly monetary policy assessment with a refreshed conditional inflation forecast
catalysts.rationale: A hold at 0.00% is near-certain and the variables are the intervention language and any revision to the 2027-2028 forecast path. It is also the last scheduled opportunity inside the horizon for the SNB to respond to a franc that has spent the autumn weakening — a hardened intervention sentence would be pair-supportive, its removal pair-negative, and a downward revision to the inflation path would reopen the negative-rate tail the quote dossier puts at 10-15%.

No projection round attached, and the meeting at which the Committee expects to have learned about 2027 pay settlements — the input the July minutes name as decisive. If private-sector regular pay is still near 2.8% and unemployment above 5.0%, the dovish resolution of a genuinely symmetric reaction function lands here, compressing the differential toward 350bp. It falls at the far edge of the strategic horizon and is the last scheduled sterling policy event inside it.

The largest recurring dollar-funding squeeze in the calendar and the most reliable seasonal source of cross-currency basis widening. It is pair-negative through two channels at once: a widening basis forces reduction of the CHF-funded carry positions that support this cross, and London's role as a large dollar-borrowing centre makes UK institutions the natural stress point, so the sterling leg is the more exposed. With the three-month EUR/USD basis last observed at only -16 to -20bp in mid-May 2026 — stale and flagged — there is more room than usual for it to widen.

assumptions: Price payload quoted verbatim: dataPoints 130; dateRange 2026-03-06 to 2026-09-03; spot 1.09224; spotDate 2026-09-03; computationRange 2007-12-21 to 2026-09-03 (4,880 weekday bars); pipSize 0.0001; weekendBarsDropped 0.

Spot date gap: spotDate is 2026-09-03, two days after the 2026-09-01 valuation date of both dossiers. The gap is disclosed rather than reconciled, and every level, target, pip figure, percentage move and distance-to-average in this report is computed against the payload spot of 1.09224. No fresher web quote has been substituted anywhere.

Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes, computed by the gated store over the whole stored history (computationRange), not over the 130 bars shown. The store is append-only and weekend-stripped on ingest. Zone distances are measured to zone midpoints.

Implied volatility is an estimate, not a quote. GBP/CHF has no listed option, so the 4.564%/4.753%/4.920% figures come from the variance identity fed a realised correlation of 0.7497 standing in for an unobservable implied one, documented to understate by 8.7%-17.8% against direct Eurex quotes (14.4% median bias across seventeen pairs). IV percentile and the 25-delta risk reversal are documented gaps.

The funding premium is a composite, not a policy differential. The gated block's -406.8bp annualised roll is computed on the CHF-base orientation of the listed futures pair; by covered interest parity it decomposes into the 375bp interest differential plus roughly 32bp of cross-currency basis, and the two cannot be separated without an OIS curve. Forward points and outrights are derived, not dealer quotes.

Sovereign yields are stale and flagged. Both 10-year legs in the payload — gilt 4.796% and Confederation 0.31% — are monthly series as of 2026-06-01, roughly 92 days old and in breach of both freshness windows. Where a fresher gilt level was required, the base dossier's 5.16% close of 28 August is used and identified as such. No Swiss 2-year yield could be sourced.

Valuation is a REER-relative proxy, not PPP. The 9.56% sterling-over-franc real-effective gap derives from BIS REER of 111.41 (GBP) and 101.69 (CHF) for June 2026, roughly 63 days old; it measures relative real standing, not absolute fair value, and the franc percentile is computed on a 30-month window only.

Bilateral trade is used as supplied. The IMF DOTS mirror asymmetry (Swiss-reported exports to the UK of USD 22.6bn against UK-reported imports of USD 12.8bn) is characteristic of non-monetary gold and re-export routing rather than a data error, so the analysis leans on the UK-reported bilateral balance of -USD 3.5bn and on the aggregate current-account differential. Bilateral investment stocks were researched separately (UK DBT factsheets, end-2023/end-2024 vintages).

Positioning vintages: headline CFTC nets for both legs are from the 28 August release covering data to 25 August. Disaggregated detail on both legs is cached to 11 August and 21 days stale; the two sets come from different CFTC report taxonomies and are not directly comparable. No pair-specific positioning series exists for GBP/CHF.

Weight adjustments: seven factors were adjusted from default, each within the ±0.05 limit, summing to exactly 1.00 on both horizons. Factor 10 was cut to the limit of the non-USD-cross guidance because a Fed repricing that damages GBP/USD is close to neutral for GBP/CHF.

Scoring mechanics and pass discipline: net_stance was derived from net_weighted_score by the stated threshold rule and applied mechanically. All ten factor stances, confidences, evidence types, weights, weighted contributions, score interpretations, rationales and G10 rankings are carried through verbatim from the settled first-pass verdict, which scored them without the price payload by design; the price data's qualification of the tactical Bullish is stated as a published disagreement rather than a re-score.

Scenario and invalidator probabilities are analyst judgements calibrated to the factor analysis and to the payload's realised volatility and zone structure; they are not derived from options-implied distributions, which are unavailable for this cross.

Consensus caveat: no GBP/CHF forecast from a primary bank research venue could be sourced. The bearish consensus figures cited are from a forecast aggregator describing a six-provider survey, not from named houses; the one named bank view (Bank of America) is reported at second hand and its numeric target is not stated. The cross-implied 1.04-1.07 range is a derivation from the two dossiers' single-leg forecast sets and inherits both legs' error.
